{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=architectural+requirements+for+artificial+intelligence+to+transition+from+episodic+memory+to+persistent+personal+identity&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6349019\", \"title\": [\"Persistent Memory Architectures for Personal Artificial Intelligence Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Recent advances in large language models have significantly expanded the capabilities of conversational artificial intelligence systems. Transformer-based architectures enable models capable of reasoning, summarization, and natural language interaction across a wide range of domains. Despite these advances, most deployed systems remain fundamentally stateless. Interactions are typically constrained by bounded context windows and lack persistent understanding of individual users. This limitation restricts the development of truly personal artificial intelligence systems capable of long-term interaction, adaptation, and cognitive support. Human cognition develops across time through accumulated experiences and reflection. Artificial intelligence systems that cannot store and interpret long-term memory remain limited in their ability to support these processes. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for persistent memory in personal artificial intelligence systems. We introduce a layered memory architecture consisting of conversational memory, semantic memory, and reflective memory. These memory layers enable artificial intelligence systems to maintain evolving representations of individuals and support long-term interaction. Persistent memory architectures may therefore represent a foundational component of next-generation personal artificial intelligence systems designed to augment human reflection, decision-making, and cognitive processes.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6349019\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005\", \"title\": [\"Situating Episodic Memory\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2016, 2, 5]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54941/ahfe1004643\", \"title\": [\"Episodic Memory with Interactive 3D Sequential Graph\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Episodic memory can be viewed as a learning process, not from existing knowledge, but from massive streams of news and episodic events. Sequences of episodic events can be used to predict future events. In this study, we assume that long-term memory can be simulated with a spatial and temporal database. We explore the 3D sequential graphs that offer a selection of methods to visualize episodic memory in the 3D space, a network of sequences of values, or a statistical summary of information about groups or subsets such as frequencies, ranges, and distributions. The graph can be accessed through a tablet, laptop, and AR/VR headsets. Users can navigate the graph with hand gestures, a game controller, or a mouse. The semantic graph is also connected to multimedia content such as video footage and spatial soundtracks because our episodic memory is multimedia. Finally, the applications of episodic memories are presented, including disastrous scenarios of laparoscopic cholecystectomy and malware distribution networks.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.54941/ahfe1004643\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1609/aaai.v39i6.32679\", \"title\": [\"Planning from Imagination: Episodic Simulation and Episodic Memory for Vision-and-Language Navigation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Humans navigate unfamiliar environments using episodic simulation and episodic memory, which facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between environments and objects. Developing an imaginative memory system inspired by human mechanisms can enhance the navigation performance of embodied agents in unseen environments. However, existing Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) agents lack a memory mechanism of this kind. To address this, we propose a novel architecture that equips agents with a reality-imagination hybrid memory system. This system enables agents to maintain and expand their memory through both imaginative mechanisms and navigation actions. Additionally, we design tailored pre-training tasks to develop the agent's imaginative capabilities. Our agent can imagine high-fidelity RGB images for future scenes, achieving state-of-the-art results in a Success rate weighted by Path Length (SPL).</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v39i6.32679\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 4, 11]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "f696ebd11dd16a37108b162b356d375d19f9e258ae492763b30db98346fe00bf", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_and_identity", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6349019", "doi:10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005", "doi:10.54941/ahfe1004643", "doi:10.1609/aaai.v39i6.32679"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6349019", "https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/10591.003.0005", "https://doi.org/10.54941/ahfe1004643", "https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v39i6.32679"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
